justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with only modest upward drift across the three horizons. For the one-day estimate, I anchored closely to what would have been the prevailing price level, assuming mean-reverting intraday dynamics and no major scheduled catalysts in the immediate window. The one-week estimate nudges slightly higher, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with longer-run trend momentum, while the one-month estimate continues that gentle upward trajectory. The incremental increases are intentionally small because the underlying asset — whatever it may be priced around 1070–1080 — shows no strong directional signal that would justify a more aggressive projection in either direction.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 54 units, capturing typical short-term volatility and the possibility of modest surprise moves. By one week, that range expands to 100 units, incorporating the possibility of a macro data release, a sentiment shift, or a liquidity-driven swing that could materially move the price without being predictable in advance. At one month, the interval stretches to 200 units, acknowledging that over that timeframe entire narratives can shift — central bank guidance, geopolitical developments, or positioning dynamics can all compound in ways that short-horizon models simply cannot foresee.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside these stated ranges. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as a stronger-than-expected economic print, a policy easing signal, or a sudden influx of institutional demand — could drive prices toward or beyond the upper bound of even the one-month interval. On the downside, a risk-off episode triggered by geopolitical escalation, a financial stability scare, or an unexpectedly hawkish policy move could break below the lower bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon. Tail events by definition fall outside 90% intervals roughly 10% of the time, so there remains meaningful probability mass in the tails that these ranges do not capture.

Finally, it is worth noting that my estimates carry model uncertainty on top of the market uncertainty already embedded in the intervals. If the underlying data I relied upon was stale, or if the asset was in the midst of a structural regime change — transitioning from low to high volatility, for instance — then my intervals could be systematically too narrow. I would treat the one-month forecast in particular with significant humility, as a range of roughly plus or minus 10% from the point estimate can still be overwhelmed by fat-tailed events that historical volatility patterns underweight.
